I’ve farmed this 1.1 mu for thirty years, ever since I married into this village. It’s barely enough to keep my own family fed, but I know every inch of it. My husband works construction in the county town and my son is away at school, so it’s mostly me and my mother‑in‑law at home. The field work falls on me, and with only three of us—and tuition and medicine to pay for—I count every yuan that goes into this soil.

Right now it’s early spring and the wheat I planted last October is greening up. Before sowing I put down about 25 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base—roughly 50 jin for the whole plot. The wheat looks okay, neither great nor terrible. For spring management I’ll topdress with about 10 kg of urea per mu when it starts jointing. Fertilizer prices went up again and urea is over 2.5 yuan per jin, so I’m not going heavier than last year. I learned my lesson two years ago when I put too much and the wheat lodged. That gives me a bit over 8 kg of nitrogen per mu for the season, which this soil can handle. I’ve farmed it long enough to know it doesn’t need a lot.

I’ll irrigate twice in spring—once when I spread the topdress so it dissolves in, and again at heading if the weather stays dry. Pumping water costs 15–20 yuan each time, and on 1.1 mu every yuan matters. I watch what Old Wang down the road does; he has a good eye for weather. I spray herbicide once in spring, and if I see aphids I’ll spray insecticide, but last year there were almost none so I saved that money. On a plot this small I sometimes just pull the big weeds by hand.

Wheat harvest will be early June, and there’s no time to waste—within a day or two I need to get the maize in the ground. I buy hybrid seed; everyone knows saved maize seed doesn’t grow well. About 2–3 jin for the whole plot, costing around 40 yuan. I’ll put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 20 kg per mu, and then side‑dress urea when the maize reaches the big‑喇叭口 stage. Two irrigations for maize if the summer rains are poor, but Hebei summers usually give us some rain, so maybe once is enough.

My biggest constraint is cash. Even though my husband sends money home, we have school fees and medical bills. I aim to keep the farm spending under 400 yuan for the year. I expect about 350 kg per mu of wheat and maybe 400 kg per mu of maize if the weather cooperates. That’s only a few hundred kilograms of each, but it means we don’t have to buy grain, and that’s the point. This land feeds us.
